item.title: What to Do if You Feel Intimidated
item.description:
Anxiety

What to Do if You Feel Intimidated

Feeling one-down in a conversation brings its own challenges.

Posted August 25, 2026

Key points
  • We all have everyday situations where we feel intimidated, anxious, and the pressure to perform.
  • Preparation, going offense, having support, and clarity about the take-away you want to create all help.
  • Take time after to mop up, but also reflect on any lessons learned.
Source: Guren-The-Thirdeye/pixabay

We’re not talking about encountering a mugger in an alley or a drunk in a bar looking for a fight. For most of us, feelings of intimidation arise in more mundane situations: the upcoming meeting with the CEO or a new client; meeting your soon-to-be in-laws at their home; the big job interview, or even the big first date with someone outside your comfort zone.

In these situations, intimidation can mean feeling nervous, feeling like you're at a disadvantage because of age or experience, or simply feeling pressure to make a good impression. What should you do? How should you handle it? Here are several suggestions to help you through.

Prepare

Preparation varies depending on the situation. For the meeting with the CEO, do your research, learn about his company, and prepare a list of questions. For the in-laws, research their likes and dislikes and their personalities. For an interview, prepare questions about the job, but also any anecdotes they may appreciate that underscore your skills and talents. For a first date, know what’s at the top of your list that you’re looking for, what your expectations are, and what you need to know most.

Dress for success

This is about making yourself comfortable, presenting yourself in a way that accurately represents you, and meeting the other’s expectations to a certain degree. Dress in the power suit for the CEO, not only to show you are competent or more experienced than your years, but also because it is what they expect. For the interview, match the work culture, or perhaps dress up a bit more than necessary. For the in-laws, wear your favorite outfit because it helps you feel more in charge.

When in doubt, go offense

People who have questions ready in a new social situation tend to feel less anxious; the same applies here. If you don’t know what to do, asking questions and shifting the conversation to the other person not only gives you important information but also helps reduce your anxiety by letting you control the conversation. So, you can ask the CEO about their goals or experience; you can ask the interviewer about benefits or salary ranges; you can ask your in-laws about their best vacation experience.

But don’t forget to talk about yourself

The ultimate aim is to have a relaxed, human-to-human conversation. Part of that is showing yourself as yourself, which means self-disclosure. With the CEO, it may be minimal—a one-liner piggybacking on their comment about starting out. For the job interview, it may be about what you really liked about your past supervisor. For the in-laws, it may be about your best vacation. For the first date, it may obviously be much more.

Decide on your ultimate goal

Consider the impression you want to make and the takeaway you ideally want them to leave the meeting with: that you and your company are professional and competent in serving their goals; that you are a flexible person with the experience to do what the job requires; that you are really, really in love with their son or daughter; that you are clear about what you’re looking for when dating, or that you’re someone who values excitement or routine.

Knowing what takeaway you hope to create can help you shape the conversation. It helps you know to skip any negative mentions of hard times at the company, past partners, or your traumatic childhood stories.

If possible, have a wing man to support you

Maybe it’s helpful to have your supervisor sit in on the CEO conversation to answer detailed questions about the company’s financial procedures, or have your partner sit next to you in case you feel flustered with the in-laws and need a bailout.

Do your best but then circle back and mop up

Follow up, not only in the traditional way—sending an email or a text thanking others for meeting with you—but also mop up any real concerns: that you didn’t know some important info the CEO asked about, and that you are researching it and will get back to them; that you realize you perhaps dominated the conversation with the in-laws or the date, or that you forgot to ask about the salary range for the position.

Reflect on you

Give yourself a few days to settle, but then reflect on your performance and presentation. Is there anything you would do differently if you did it over? Are there triggers that prompt you to overreact? Are there skills you need to develop to create the impression you hoped to create?

This is like next-day quarterbacking; assess, when calm and rational, any lessons learned about you, how your anxiety affects you, and what you need to be careful to do or not do in future situations.

New situations are always opportunities to learn new skills and to learn about yourself. Fortunately, life is about learning, and learning is a process of elimination—making mistakes and learning from them.

What do you need most to learn?

item.title: Women, Wealth, and the Rules We Inherit
item.description:
Gender

Women, Wealth, and the Rules We Inherit

How culture and family shape the stories women inherit about money and success.

Posted August 25, 2026

Key points
  • Women’s financial independence is recent, and inherited beliefs about money can outlast legal change.
  • Success does not erase the barriers women may still face around money, authority, and power.
  • For women of color, money can also reflect culture, family obligation, migration, and class mobility.
  • The goal is not to reject inherited values, but to choose which ones still belong in our lives.
The author and her mother
Source: Huong Diep

For Women’s Equality Day, I’ve been thinking about the unspoken rules women inherit about money, power, and taking up space—and just how much more complicated those rules are for women of color.

August 26 marks the 1920 certification of the 19th Amendment. It was a huge milestone, but progress didn't happen evenly. Black women faced discriminatory voting restrictions for decades after, Native American women weren't granted U.S. citizenship until 1924, and many Asian immigrant women remained entirely excluded.

I recently learned about Mabel Ping-Hua Lee, a Chinese immigrant who marched for suffrage as a teenager in New York. She spent years advocating for voting rights despite knowing Chinese exclusion laws meant she couldn't actually vote herself. That contradiction stayed with me: What does it mean to fight for a seat at a table you aren't even allowed to sit at?

Today, women have access to opportunities that Lee’s generation could not have imagined. Unfortunately, the limiting messages about what we should want, how ambitious we can be, and how much space we can take up still persists.

The Rules We Learned Early On

I grew up in a traditional Vietnamese household where being a “good girl” meant being obedient, dutiful, humble, and quiet. Unfortunately for my mother, I loved asking questions. I wanted to know why my younger brother could run around outside freely or go on sleepovers when I couldn't. The answer was usually simple: “Because you’re a girl.”

As an adult, I look back with a lot more compassion. My mother was passing down the exact values handed to her, driven by real fear and a protective instinct. And not everything she taught me was something I wanted to discard—she taught me how to read a room, listen carefully, work hard, and put the collective before myself. I still care deeply about those values.

Things got complicated when I entered professional spaces operating by a set of completely different rules, rules that I never learned. Suddenly, success went to the people who advocated for themselves, negotiated, spoke up early, and assumed they belonged in the room.

This is a central conundrum for many of my clients: How do you ask for more when you were raised to just be grateful for what you have? How do you speak up when humility is the core of who you are?

Women and Money

I recently read Cary Carbonaro’s Women and Wealth. I appreciated her honesty about how, even as a highly successful financial advisor, she kept running into systemic roadblocks. Her individual success didn't magically rewrite the system or erase the fact that financial structures were never built for women.

It’s astonishing how recent basic financial rights actually are.

Bella Abzug, who pushed to recognize Women’s Equality Day, also fought discrimination in credit. Before the Equal Credit Opportunity Act passed in the 1970s, banks routinely required a husband or male relative to co-sign on a woman's account. That was only a few decades ago.

So while women are now allowed to build businesses, manage portfolios, and act as primary breadwinners, that does not mean our inherited scripts have changed. I've spoken with too many women who out-earn their partner but still feel guilty spending on themselves, who inherit wealth and question if they deserve it, or who run a successful company while wondering if they're "smart enough."

This is why financial psychology matters so much to me. Financial literacy matters, but so does unpacking what we attach to money: safety, obligation, loyalty, and our definition of what a “good person” does with wealth.

Beyond Gender

For women of color, the layers run even deeper. Race, immigration, class, and family history shape every financial decision. I sit with clients navigating the heavy dynamics of out-earning their parents, dealing with class mobility, or feeling exhausted by financial filial duty after growing up believing that they had to "repay" their families for their sacrifices.

Also, what sometimes gets mislabeled as a “lack of confidence” usually has a much longer backstory. A woman might hesitate out of respect for an elder, or stay quiet because keeping family harmony was the highest virtue growing up. Before telling women to just be more assertive, we need to understand the rules they learned and what those rules were trying to protect.

What I Am Still Unlearning

My mother was thirty-six weeks pregnant with me when she boarded a boat to leave Vietnam without knowing where she would end up. She wanted a better future for her daughter.

I have opportunities she never dreamed of, but I also carry inherited fears and instincts. That is part of what draws me to this work, especially with women navigating major life and financial transitions: inheritance, divorce, career changes, caregiving, sudden wealth, entrepreneurship, or becoming the first person in their family to build significant wealth.

I am interested in what happens when our circumstances change, but some of the old rules follow us.

I want us to get curious enough to ask: Which rules still fit? Which ones still feel like mine? And which ones can I thank for getting me this far before saying, "Thank you, but I don’t need you anymore."
